paragraphs: One must make a great effort to seek out an opportunity for zimun (the invitation formula before Birkat HaMazon said when three or more have eaten together), for it is a great thing that thereby removes and drives away the Sitra Achra (the 'Other Side,' the force of impurity), as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote. And just as it is a mitzvah to seek out three in order to make the zimun, so it is an even greater mitzvah to seek out ten in order to make the zimun with mention of God's Name. One of them should say first: 'Give us leave and let us bless the supreme, holy King, and with the permission of the supreme, holy King let us bless...' and on Shabbat he says 'and with the permission of Shabbat the Queen,' and on a Yom Tov he adds 'and with the permission of the Yom Tov, the holy guest,' and on Sukkot he adds 'and with the permission of the seven supreme, holy Ushpizin (guests).' Those seated answer, 'Blessed is He of whose bounty we have eaten,' and the one leading the zimun repeats and says, 'Blessed is He of whose bounty we have eaten...' And if there are ten, one should not say 'Nevarech Leloheinu' (with the letter lamed) but rather 'Nevarech Eloheinu' (without the lamed), as it is written, 'In assemblies bless God' (Psalms 68:27), 'Bless our God, O peoples' (Psalms 66:8) — without a lamed, for the lamed is said only in expressions of song and thanksgiving, such as 'Sing to the Lord' (Exodus 15:21, and elsewhere) and 'Give thanks to the Lord' (Isaiah 12:4, and elsewhere).

clarification.explanation: One must exert effort and seek an opportunity to make a zimun (to bless Birkat HaMazon with three), for this is a great thing that removes and drives away the power of impurity, as the holy Ari wrote. And just as there is a mitzvah to seek out three in order to make a zimun, so there is an even greater mitzvah to seek out ten in order to make the zimun with mention of God's Name. In such a case, one of those seated opens and says, 'Give us leave and let us bless the supreme, holy King, and with the permission of the supreme, holy King let us bless...' (an Aramaic formula requesting permission from the Holy One, blessed be He, to bless) — and on Shabbat they add 'and with the permission of Shabbat the Queen,' on Yom Tov 'and with the permission of the Yom Tov, the holy guest,' and on Sukkot they also add 'and with the permission of the seven supreme, holy Ushpizin' (in remembrance of the Ushpizin — the holy guests hosted in the sukkah). The rest of those seated answer, 'Blessed is He of whose bounty we have eaten,' and the leader of the zimun repeats and also says, 'Blessed is He of whose bounty we have eaten.' And when there are ten, one does not say 'Nevarech Leloheinu' (with the letter lamed) but 'Nevarech Eloheinu' (without the lamed) — as appears in the verses of Psalms, 'In assemblies bless God' and 'Bless our God, O peoples,' where there is no lamed. The lamed appears only in expressions of song and thanksgiving such as 'Sing to the Lord' and 'Give thanks to the Lord.'
takeaways: It is worthwhile to seek an opportunity to make a zimun with three, and even better — to make a zimun with ten, with mention of God's Name.
In a zimun of ten, the formula is changed to 'Nevarech Eloheinu' without the letter lamed.
On Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Sukkot, appropriate additions are made to the opening formula of the zimun.

paragraphs: If the leader of the zimun erred with ten and those answering did not mention 'Eloheinu,' they cannot go back; but if they have not yet answered after him, he may go back and lead the zimun again with the Name. And if the leader did not mention the Name but those answering did mention it, he answers after them and mentions the Name, since all of them have already mentioned it. But if he did not mention the Name and those answering also did not mention it, then he too, when he answers after them, will not mention the Name.

clarification.explanation: If the leader of the zimun erred in a zimun of ten (that is, he did not mention God's Name), and those answering already answered after him without mentioning the Name — it cannot be corrected retroactively. But if those answering have not yet managed to answer after him, the leader can retract and lead the zimun again while mentioning the Name. And if the leader himself did not mention the Name, but those answering did mention it in their response, then the leader, when he answers after them afterward, does mention the Name, since everyone has already mentioned it. But if both the leader and those answering did not mention the Name at all — when the leader answers after them afterward, he will not mention the Name (since the matter has already been missed).
takeaways: If everyone erred and did not mention God's Name in a zimun of ten, there is no way to correct it after the fact.
There is a possibility of correction only if those answering have not yet answered after the leader.

paragraphs: Householders who each live in his own separate room, and in the summer months it is their custom for all of them to set their tables in a courtyard or on a roof for the day's breeze, with each one eating at his own table — if they sat down initially with the intent to join together, then they do join together for the zimun. But if they did not sit down initially with the intent to join together, the matter is in doubt. Therefore, in any such case, it is good to be careful that they sit down initially with the intent to join together for the blessing of the zimun, and then they bless the zimun according to all opinions. See 'Ot Hi LeOlam,' Ma'arechet HaZayin, page 126.

clarification.explanation: When several householders each live in his own separate room, and in the summer months they are all accustomed to sit and eat together in a courtyard or on a roof for the day's breeze, with each one eating from his own table — if they sat down initially with the intention of joining together for the matter of the zimun, they do join together and bless a single zimun for all of them. But if they did not sit down with such an intention from the outset, there is doubt as to whether they join together. Therefore it is proper to be careful and to decide explicitly in advance to sit with the intention of joining together, so that they can bless the zimun without any question.
takeaways: In order for several people sitting separately to join together for a single zimun, they must decide on this in advance.
It is preferable to clarify the intention to join together in advance, in order to remove any doubt.

paragraphs: One who ate in a group that became obligated in zimun is not permitted to bless for himself first, even if he has urgent business, and if he did so, he committed a transgression. And if he is in a hurry to leave, if it is possible for him to persuade them to stop and make the zimun together with him, that is best; and if not, he is obligated to wait for them until they finish. Likewise, four or five may not split up, since all of them became obligated together in one zimun. But six may split up, since a zimun will remain for each group. However, ten may not split up, since they became obligated in the mention of the Name. And if they are twenty, they may split up, since each group will have ten to mention the Name.

clarification.explanation: One who ate in a group that became obligated in a zimun is not permitted to rush and bless Birkat HaMazon for himself before the rest of the group, even if he has an urgent matter. And if he did so, he transgressed a prohibition. If he is in a hurry to leave, it is best to try to persuade the others to stop and make the zimun together with him right away; and if they did not agree, he is obligated to wait for them until the meal is finished. Similarly, a group of four or five who ate together may not split up, since all of them already became obligated together in one zimun. But if they are six, they are permitted to split into two groups, since in each group enough people (three) remain for a zimun. On the other hand, if they are ten, they may not split up, since they already became obligated together in a zimun with mention of the Name (which requires ten). But if they are twenty, they are permitted to split into two groups, since ten who can mention the Name will remain in each group.
takeaways: One is not permitted to rush and bless Birkat HaMazon alone before the group that became obligated together in a zimun.
A group of 4-5 cannot split up; a group of 6 can; a group of 10 is forbidden to split up; a group of 20 is permitted.

paragraphs: Three who sat down to eat, and one of them ate mezonot foods or other fruits requiring only a concluding blessing, while the other two ate actual bread — they may make a zimun over him. However, it is good to make an effort to press him to eat bread as well. See Chayim Sha'al, part 1.

clarification.explanation: Three who sat down to eat together, and one of them ate only mezonot foods (cakes and the like) or fruits, for which he became obligated only in a different kind of concluding blessing, while the other two actually ate bread — the two who ate bread can make a zimun and include the one who ate mezonot foods or fruit as well. Nevertheless, it is proper to try to persuade him to eat some bread too, so that the zimun will be more complete and more beautifully performed.
takeaways: One who did not eat bread can still join a zimun with two who ate bread.
It is preferable to persuade him to eat a bit of bread, for the enhancement of the mitzvah.

paragraphs: Three who sat down to eat, and one of them jumped ahead and blessed by himself — even though he committed a transgression by doing so — nevertheless the other two can make a zimun over him and thereby fulfill their obligation of zimun, while he does not fulfill it. In what case does this apply? Where all three ate bread. But if the two ate bread and the third ate mezonot or the like, and he jumped ahead and recited the concluding blessing — the two can no longer make a zimun over him.

clarification.explanation: Three who sat down to eat, and one of them rushed and blessed Birkat HaMazon for himself before the others finished (even though in doing so he transgressed, as stated in the previous halacha) — nevertheless, the two remaining can make a zimun and include him in their zimun, and they fulfill their obligation of zimun, but he himself does not fulfill it (since he already blessed). This applies specifically when all three ate bread. But if the other two ate bread and the third ate only mezonot or the like, and he rushed and recited a concluding blessing for himself — the two can no longer make a zimun and include him (since he is not obligated in the zimun as they are).
takeaways: One who rushed and blessed alone still 'serves' to allow the remaining two to join for a zimun, provided all three ate bread.
If the one who jumped ahead ate only mezonot and not bread, he can no longer join the zimun.

paragraphs: Two who ate together and finished, and a third came: as long as they have not said 'Give us leave and let us bless,' or have not washed their hands for mayim acharonim, they are obligated to give him food so that he may join them. But if they said 'Give us leave and let us bless' or washed their hands, he does not join them. However, if they said only 'Let us wash our hands' — since they did not say 'and let us bless,' he does join. And there is one who wrote that even if they washed their hands or said 'Give us leave and let us bless,' so that he does not join — nevertheless it is a mitzvah for them to wash their hands, bless, and eat a little, for the sake of the zimun. Go and learn how beloved the mitzvah of zimun is, as mentioned in all this in Chesed LeAlafim, of blessed memory; see there.

clarification.explanation: Two who ate together and finished, and a third came: as long as they have not said 'Give us leave and let us bless' and have not washed mayim acharonim — they are obligated to give him food so that he may join them for the zimun. But if they have already said 'Give us leave and let us bless' or washed their hands — he does not join. Nevertheless, if they said only 'Let us wash our hands' (without 'and let us bless') — he still joins. And there is one who wrote that even if they washed their hands or said 'Give us leave and let us bless,' so that he does not join — it is still a mitzvah for them to wash their hands, bless, and eat a little, in order to make a zimun. Go and learn how beloved the mitzvah of zimun is (Chesed LeAlafim).
takeaways: When two have finished and a third arrives, they must give him food so he may join the zimun, as long as they have not said 'Give us leave and let us bless' and have not washed mayim acharonim.
If they said only 'let us wash our hands' without 'and let us bless,' he joins; and even if he cannot join, it is a mitzvah for them to eat a little in order to make a zimun.

paragraphs: Seven ate bread, and three ate vegetables, or fruit the size of an olive, or drank a revi'it of any kind of beverage other than water — they join for the zimun. This applies specifically to seven or more, but not to six, since a clearly recognizable majority is required. And the one who joins in this way must recite his own concluding blessing over what he ate or drank, and he is not exempted by the Birkat HaMazon of the others.

clarification.explanation: If seven people ate bread, and three others ate only vegetables, or fruit the size of an olive, or drank a revi'it of any kind of beverage (other than water) — they can join the zimun with the seven. But this is true specifically when there are seven who ate bread or more, and not when there are only six, since a clearly recognizable majority of those who ate bread is required. One who joins in this way (without bread) must recite his own concluding blessing over what he ate or drank, and he is not exempted from this blessing by the Birkat HaMazon of those who ate bread.
takeaways: One who did not eat bread can join the zimun only if there are at least seven who ate bread.
The one who joins must still recite his own concluding blessing over what he ate, separately from Birkat HaMazon.

paragraphs: Three who ate together — the two are not obligated to interrupt for the one in order to make the zimun, unless he is their father or their teacher. But the one is obligated to interrupt for the two against his will; he must answer the zimun with them and interrupt his eating until they say 'Who feeds all,' and afterward he returns to his eating. All this is according to the strict letter of the law. Nevertheless, since there are those who say that the one who interrupts for the two must go back and wash his hands and recite the blessing of HaMotzi again — it is therefore good that they not do this, forcing him to interrupt for their sake, but rather that they wait until he too finishes, and they bless together, so that this does not enter into doubtful matters of conflicting blessings from the outset.

clarification.explanation: Three who ate together — the two are not obligated to interrupt their eating in order to wait for the one who is still eating, unless he is their father or their teacher (in which case there is an obligation of honor). But the one (if he has not finished) is obligated to interrupt against his will for the sake of the two who finished — he must answer the zimun with them and interrupt his eating until saying 'Who feeds all,' and only afterward return to eating. All this is according to the strict letter of the law. Nevertheless, since there are opinions that the one who interrupts must go back and wash his hands and recite HaMotzi anew — it is better in practice not to force him to interrupt for their sake, but rather to wait until he too finishes, and then all bless together. In this way, one avoids introducing doubt regarding conflicting matters of blessings.
takeaways: By strict law, a lone individual is obligated to interrupt his eating in order to answer the zimun for the two who finished.
In practice it is recommended to wait for him to finish, in order to avoid doubts regarding blessings.

paragraphs: If there are four, and the three interrupted for the sake of the one, they do not go back and make a zimun over what they eat afterward, since the zimun has already 'flown' from them. But if there are ten, and the seven interrupted for the sake of the three, the seven do go back and make a zimun afterward over what they eat, because the three could have made a zimun for themselves and did not need these seven to join them except for the mention of the Name; therefore these seven can make a zimun without mention of the Name over what they eat after that zimun.

clarification.explanation: If there were four people, and three of them interrupted their eating in order to make a zimun for the fourth (as explained in the previous halacha) — they will not go back and make a zimun again over what they eat afterward, since the zimun has already 'flown' (passed) from them and they have already fulfilled it. But if there were ten, and seven of them interrupted for the sake of three — the seven do go back and make a zimun again afterward over what they eat, because in this case the three could have made a zimun for themselves without any need for the seven, and they only needed to join with the seven in order to complete a quorum of ten for the mention of the Name. Therefore the seven can make a zimun again afterward, only this time without mention of the Name.
takeaways: In a group of four that interrupted to make a zimun, the zimun is 'finished' and does not recur.
In a group of ten that interrupted to make a zimun for the sake of three, the seven can make a zimun again afterward (without mention of the Name).

paragraphs: A minor who has reached the age of understanding (chinuch), which is about nine years old — Maran, of blessed memory, ruled that he joins the zimun, and the Rema wrote that the custom is not to include him until he is truly an adult. Here in our city of Baghdad, the custom follows the opinion of Maran, of blessed memory. Nevertheless, it is good to make an effort to include a genuine adult where possible.

clarification.explanation: A minor who has reached the 'age of understanding' (an age at which he has a certain degree of comprehension, around nine years old) — Maran (Rabbi Yosef Karo) ruled that he does join the zimun. The Rema wrote that there are those who follow the custom of not including him until he is truly an adult (bar mitzvah). In the city of Baghdad (the city where the Ben Ish Chai lived), the custom was to follow the opinion of Maran, including even a minor who reached the age of understanding. Nevertheless, when possible, it is proper to make an effort to include a genuine adult instead.
takeaways: In Baghdad the custom was to include in the zimun even a minor from the age of understanding (about 9), following the opinion of Maran.
When there is a possibility, it is preferable to include a genuine adult.

paragraphs: A mute person who hears but does not speak — even though he answers the zimun by thought and also blesses by thought, and we hold that thought is effective like speech in a case of duress — nevertheless, since he is not fit for actual speech, there is room for doubt regarding him; therefore he does not join the zimun. See Eshel Avraham, siman 199, se'if katan 8. But a deaf person who speaks but does not hear, if he concentrates, does join the zimun.

clarification.explanation: A mute person who hears well but cannot speak — although he can answer the zimun and bless by thought alone (mental intention), and it is known that in a case of duress (when there is no choice) thought is considered equivalent to speech — nevertheless, since he cannot actually speak, there is doubt as to whether he is fit to join the zimun, and therefore in practice he is not included in the zimun. By contrast, a deaf person who can speak but does not hear does join the zimun, provided he understands and directs his mind to what he is saying.
takeaways: A mute person (who cannot speak) does not join the zimun, due to doubt, even though he can express it mentally.
A deaf person who speaks and concentrates does join the zimun.

paragraphs: Women — although all agree that a zimun is not made over them (by men) — nevertheless, there are those who say that they are obligated to make a zimun among themselves, and there are those who say it is optional: if they wish, they make a zimun among themselves. Given this, it is proper for every person to teach the women of his household to make a zimun among themselves when they eat with three. But they should not make the zimun with mention of the Name, even if they are a hundred.

clarification.explanation: Regarding women — everyone agrees that men cannot make a zimun on their behalf (that is, they are not included in a men's zimun). But there is a dispute as to whether they themselves, when three women eat together, are obligated to make a zimun among themselves: some say they are obligated, and some say it is only optional — if they wish, they make a zimun among themselves. Despite the dispute, it is proper for every person to teach the members of his household — the women — to make a habit of making a zimun among themselves when three of them eat together. But in any case, even if they are a hundred women, they do not make the zimun with mention of God's Name (which is reserved for a zimun of ten men).
takeaways: Three women eating together should properly make a zimun among themselves.
Women, even if there are a hundred of them, do not make the zimun with mention of God's Name.

paragraphs: Members of a household who eat together: the greatest among them breaks the bread, and he himself leads the zimun. And if there is a guest present, the host breaks the bread, but the guest blesses and leads the zimun. And if there is a kohen present, it is a mitzvah to give him precedence, if there is no Torah scholar present; and a kohen who is a Torah scholar — it is a mitzvah to give him precedence over a Torah scholar who is not a kohen. However, if the kohen wishes to grant honor to that Torah scholar, he is permitted to do so, and the scholar then says 'with the permission of the kohen.' And there are those who say that a Levite, too, should be given precedence over a Yisrael in this order, but the custom has not followed this.

clarification.explanation: Members of a household who eat together — the greatest among them breaks the bread (cuts it and recites HaMotzi), and he himself also leads the blessing of the zimun. If there is a guest in the house, the host is the one who breaks the bread, but the guest is the one who leads the zimun (a custom of honoring the guest). If there is a kohen among those present, he should be given precedence to lead the zimun, unless there is a Torah scholar present (who takes precedence over an ordinary kohen). And a kohen who is also a Torah scholar — it is a mitzvah to give him precedence even over a Torah scholar who is not a kohen. Nevertheless, if the kohen (the Torah scholar) himself wishes to yield and grant honor to the other Torah scholar, he is permitted to do so, and then the Torah scholar leads the zimun saying 'with the permission of the kohen.' There are those who say that a Levite, too, should be given precedence over an ordinary Yisrael in this order of precedence for leading the zimun, but this has not been the accepted practice.
takeaways: In a house with a guest — the host breaks the bread, and the guest leads the zimun.
The order of precedence for leading the zimun: a kohen who is a Torah scholar, then a Torah scholar, then an ordinary kohen.
A kohen may waive his honor and let a Torah scholar lead the zimun 'with his permission.'
